title: Best CAD/CAM Software for Business in India (2026)
excerpt: How to choose CAD and CAM software in India: 2D drafting, 3D modelling and toolpaths, with the Autodesk range we quote and questions for any CAM supplier.
body:
There is no single best CAD/CAM package for every Indian business. A drawing office, a CNC job shop and a product-design studio each use different tools, and money is wasted when one product is bought for all of them. This guide separates the three layers: 2D drafting, 3D modelling and CAM (the software that turns a model into machine instructions). It then shows where the Autodesk products TechZoid quotes fit, and gives you questions to put to any CAM supplier, including ones we do not sell.

## CAD and CAM are different jobs

**CAD** (computer-aided design) is where the part or drawing is created. **CAM** (computer-aided manufacturing) takes that geometry and produces toolpaths: the cutter movements, speeds and feeds that a CNC machine follows. A **post-processor** then translates those toolpaths into the exact dialect your machine controller understands. Many failed purchases come from treating these as one decision.

Start with five questions.

1. What is the deliverable: a drawing, a 3D model, a building model, or a machined part?
2. Which discipline: architecture, civil, mechanical, product design or tooling?
3. Who do you exchange files with, and in which format?
4. How many people need the software, and how often does each open it?
5. What machines and controllers do you run, if you are making parts?

Our [CAD software category page](/cad-software) lists everything we sell in this area, and [BIM software](/bim-software) covers building-model tools.

## Three layers: 2D drafting, 3D modelling, CAM

**2D drafting** produces drawings: plans, layouts, fabrication sketches and documentation. It remains the daily work of many interior, electrical and fabrication teams. If nobody needs a 3D model, you do not need a 3D package.

**3D modelling** builds solid or surface models of parts and assemblies, checks fit and motion, and generates drawings from the model. It is the base for any serious CNC work, because CAM needs a clean 3D model to cut.

**CAM** adds machining strategy. In 2.5D work (pockets, profiles, drilled holes) a modest package is enough. In 3-axis surface machining, and especially in 4- and 5-axis work, the toolpath engine, collision checking and simulation become the main purchase criteria.

## 2D drafting: AutoCAD LT and AutoCAD

If your output is drawings, start here. **AutoCAD LT** is cost-effective 2D CAD for drafting, drawing and documentation. **AutoCAD** is the full product, with 3D modelling and rendering, DWG comparison, sheet sets and seven industry toolsets (Architecture, Mechanical, Electrical, MEP, Map 3D, Plant 3D and Raster Design) included, plus the web and mobile apps. The decision is covered in [AutoCAD vs AutoCAD LT](/blog/autocad-vs-autocad-lt): pure 2D, choose LT; 3D, toolsets or automation, choose AutoCAD. For pricing context, read [AutoCAD subscription price in India](/blog/autocad-subscription-price-in-india). Site engineers who only mark up drawings can use [AutoCAD Web](/products/autocad-web) in a browser, a lower-cost way to cover occasional users.

## 3D modelling and CNC work: Inventor and Fusion

[Autodesk Inventor](/products/autodesk-inventor) provides product design and engineering tools for 3D mechanical design, simulation, visualisation and documentation. It suits engineering firms designing assemblies, machinery and components.

[Autodesk Fusion](/products/fusion-360) combines mechanical design, manufacturing toolpaths, simulation and electronics in one cloud-connected application. For a job shop or a small product-design team, the integration is the point: the model, the toolpath and the setup sheet live together, so a design change flows to the CAM toolpath without re-importing geometry. It runs on Windows and macOS and needs a persistent internet connection for cloud data. Some advanced manufacturing, simulation and generative design capabilities are licensed as separate extensions, so tell us your machine types and axis count before we quote. Fusion is also offered in separate design and manufacturing configurations, which we can explain against your workflow.

For buildings and infrastructure, [Revit](/products/revit) and [Civil 3D](/products/autodesk-civil-3d) cover BIM and site design, compared in [Revit vs AutoCAD](/blog/revit-vs-autocad). They are Windows-only and need real workstations.

## Two workflows compared

**CNC job shop.** The input is usually a customer's model or drawing in whatever format they send, and the output is a programme that runs on a specific machine. The priorities are: importing messy geometry, fast setup of fixtures and tools, a reliable post-processor for each machine, and simulation to avoid a crashed spindle. Native design tools matter less than CAM quality and speed of programming. Seats are few, and the programmer is often the owner.

**Product-design studio or machine builder.** The input is an idea or a specification, and the output is a documented design that might go to an outside shop. Parametric modelling, assemblies, drawings and bills of materials matter most. CAM may be used only for prototypes, so an integrated package like Fusion can be enough, while a team building complex machinery may prefer Inventor and hand toolpaths to a shop.

Many businesses sit in between. List people by role and give each the lightest product that does the job.

## What to ask about CAM: post-processors, simulation, data

Whichever CAM product you evaluate, ask these in writing and test them on your own part.

- **Post-processors.** Is there a tested post for each of your machine and controller combinations? Who edits it when you change a controller or add a rotary axis? Is the post editable by you, or only by the publisher? A weak post forces manual editing of code at the machine.
- **Simulation.** Does it simulate material removal, the holder and the machine kinematics, or only the tool? Does it flag gouges and collisions before you run a part? Simulation is a cheaper teacher than scrap.
- **Toolpath capability.** Which strategies suit your materials and your axis count? Ask for a demonstration with a part from your own shop, not a showroom sample.
- **Tool and cutting data.** Can tool libraries and feeds-and-speeds be shared across programmers?
- **File exchange.** Which native and neutral formats (STEP, IGES, Parasolid, DXF/DWG) import cleanly, and does it keep associativity when the model changes?
- **Data management.** Where do models, toolpaths and revisions live, who can edit, and what happens when two people open the same file? Cloud-based data management helps teams but needs internet; local approaches need your own backup and discipline.
- **Licence terms.** Is it named-user or machine-locked, and can a seat be reassigned when someone leaves?

## Other CAM tools you may meet

We sell Autodesk, so this is description, not a recommendation. Widely used CAM tools from other publishers include Mastercam, SolidCAM (which works inside SolidWorks), Siemens NX CAM and hyperMILL, as well as CAM modules inside other CAD systems. Customers and sub-contractors often standardise on one of these, and file compatibility with them can be a legitimate reason to choose differently. Evaluate them with the same questions above, and check their current capabilities directly with each publisher. If your sector already standardises on another package, ask us about the Autodesk side only for what you need to interoperate.

## Collections and occasional users

A collection bundles several products for one named user. The [AEC Collection](/products/aec-collection) suits building and infrastructure teams, and the [Product Design & Manufacturing Collection](/products/autodesk-product-design-manufacturing-collection) is the manufacturing equivalent. The commercial rule: with one product per user, standalone is cheaper; with two it is roughly break-even; with three or more a collection usually wins. See [the AEC Collection explained](/blog/autodesk-aec-collection-explained). For someone who needs a product a few days a year, Autodesk Flex lets you prepay tokens and draw them down; it is priced on enquiry, and the arithmetic is in [Flex versus named-user subscriptions](/blog/autodesk-flex-versus-named-user-subscriptions).

## Which should you pick? Examples

- **Interior design studio, six people, 2D layouts:** AutoCAD LT.
- **Architecture practice delivering BIM:** Revit, or the AEC Collection if AutoCAD and coordination tools are also needed.
- **Two-machine CNC job shop that programmes customer parts:** a CAM-capable package such as Fusion, after testing posts for your controllers and checking whether you need extensions.
- **Machine builder designing assemblies:** Inventor, with toolpaths done in-house or by a shop.
- **Start-up making consumer hardware:** Fusion for design through prototype CAM.
- **Site engineers who mark up drawings:** AutoCAD Web.

## Hardware and file-format checks

CAD and CAM are hungry. AutoCAD asks for 16 GB of RAM at minimum, with 32 GB recommended for large drawings and 3D work, and a DirectX 12 capable GPU. Revit and Civil 3D are Windows only. Fusion is lighter, with a stated minimum of 8 GB of RAM and 16 GB recommended, but needs a persistent internet connection for cloud data. If you are specifying new machines, our workstation range is worth a look, and you should check Autodesk's current requirements first. DWG remains the common currency for drawings; for machined parts, confirm whether customers send STEP or native files.

## Licensing, GST and buying in India

All products above are licensed per named user: one subscription, one person, reassignable when someone leaves. Multi-year terms are generally cheaper per year than annual renewal, and monthly or multi-year terms can be quoted on request. Understand the model in [Autodesk named-user licensing: what changed](/blog/autodesk-named-user-licensing-what-changed). Every order carries a GST invoice at 18%, usually claimable as input credit by GST-registered buyers. To see everything in one place, view our [price list](/price-list), then [ask for a quotation](/enquiry) with the number of users per role and your machine types.

faqs.question: What is the best CAD/CAM software for a small business in India?
faqs.answer: It depends on the work. For 2D drawings, AutoCAD LT is the economical start. For 3D and automation, choose AutoCAD. Mechanical design points to Inventor or Fusion, and a job shop that programmes CNC parts should test CAM, posts and simulation on its own part before buying.

faqs.question: What is a post-processor and why does it matter?
faqs.answer: A post-processor converts toolpaths into the code your machine controller understands. A poor one means editing code by hand at the machine. Ask who writes and maintains the post for your machine and controller, and test it on a real part.

faqs.question: Do I need separate CAD and CAM software?
faqs.answer: Not always. Integrated packages such as Fusion combine modelling and toolpaths, which can suit job shops and product teams. Complex multi-axis work may justify a specialist CAM product. Decide after testing your own parts.

faqs.question: Does this guide cover all CAD and CAM software?
faqs.answer: No. We quote the Autodesk products listed and describe other widely used CAM tools only in general terms. We do not rank them. If your customers use something else, compatibility is a valid reason to follow them.

faqs.question: Do Autodesk subscriptions include GST?
faqs.answer: Website prices exclude GST. GST is 18% on software and is added on the invoice, usually claimable as input credit by GST-registered businesses. A written quotation fixes the final price, since website prices are tentative.

faqs.question: Should I buy a collection instead of individual products?
faqs.answer: Only if each person truly uses two or more products in it. With one product per user, standalone costs less; around two it is close to break-even, and with three or more a collection usually wins. We compare against your usage before quoting.
